Empirical Research Plan:  The Dust Bowl, Agricultural Productivity, and Local Economic Adjustment  

==================================================================
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy:  Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension (“dynamic DID”).

Why this fits  

• Clear treatment date: the drought‐and‐wind‐erosion shock that crystallised between 1934 and 1936.  
• Cross-sectional variation in treatment intensity: some counties were heavily eroded; others in the same broad agricultural economy were not.  
• Long balanced panel of counties (≈1920–1970) enables pre-trend checks and dynamic post-treatment paths.  
• Environmental shock is plausibly exogenous to county-level economic policy choices, making DID credible once common-trend issues are addressed.

We will also exploit continuous treatment intensity (Dust-Bowl Severity Index) and, for robustness, a border-county matched-pair design that approximates an RDD around the geographic edge of the Dust-Bowl footprint.



==================================================================
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment Variable  

TREATEDc   = 1 if county c’s Dust-Bowl severity index (DBI) ≥ p75 of the national distribution during 1934–36  
           = 0 otherwise.  

• DBI is constructed from dust-storm frequency, topsoil loss measurements, and drought-severity scores in the 1934 Soil Conservation Service reports.  
• In continuous specifications we use DBI itself.

Control Group  

Counties below the 75th percentile of DBI, excluding (i) counties in the same climatic zone whose DBI > p25 (to create clearer separation) and (ii) counties that received comparable New Deal agricultural relief specifically earmarked for drought damage before 1934 (to avoid differential policy confounding).  

Treatment Timing  

Postt = 1 for years ≥ 1934 (baseline), with event-study leads/lags from t = –10 (1924) to t = +40 (1974).  

Running Variable / Cut-off  

Not applicable for the core DID. (In the border-county robustness RDD, distance to the mapped Dust-Bowl boundary is the running variable; cutoff = 0.)



==================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Pre-Trends  
In absence of the Dust Bowl, treated and control counties’ agricultural productivity and economic outcomes would have evolved in parallel.  
Plausibility: neighbouring Great Plains counties shared markets and technology. We verify with 1920–33 trends and placebo tests on 1920s rainfall shocks.

A2. No Anticipatory Behaviour Pre-1934  
Farmers could not foresee the severity of the 1934–36 drought/erosion and adjust land use beforehand.  
Plausibility: Dust storms were unprecedented; agronomic advice at the time did not predict multi-year erosion.

A3. Stable Composition / Migration as an Outcome, not a Confounder  
Out-migration is part of the treatment channel, not a violation, as long as we measure outcomes at the county level (per acre or per resident) and interpret ITT effects.

A4. No Differential Concurrent Shocks  
Other New Deal programs or wartime mobilization did not differentially target treated counties conditional on controls (addressed with year×state FE and county-specific weather controls).

A5. SUTVA (no spillovers across counties)  
Dust storms could cross county borders; we mitigate by clustering at climate-zone level, and by sensitivity that drops 25-mile buffer counties.



==================================================================
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Differential Pre-Treatment Trends  
   • Test: event-study coefficients for t ≤ –1 should be ~0.  
   • Remedy: include county-specific linear trends; adopt matched-pair DID within homogeneous soil zones.

Threat 2: Policy Confounding (AAA subsidies, soil-conservation aid)  
   • Collect county‐year payments from Agricultural Adjustment Administration (AAA).  
   • Control for AAA dollars per acre; interact with Postt.  
   • Instrument severity with ex-ante wind-erosion susceptibility index to purge aid endogeneity.

Threat 3: Selective Migration Biasing Denominator of per-capita Outcomes  
   • Estimate both per-acre and per-capita outcomes.  
   • Use population as a separate dependent variable (to quantify migration) rather than conditioning on it.  
   • Apply Lee bounds where relevant to show robustness to attrition.



==================================================================
5. R Code Outline  
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages ----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)    # fast data handling
library(fixest)        # econometrics with FE
library(did)           # callaway-sant'anna for staggered timing (if needed)
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Data --------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three CSVs: county_ag.csv, county_demo.csv, county_econ.csv
ag   <- fread("county_ag.csv")     # yields, acres, etc.
demo <- fread("county_demo.csv")   # population, migration flows
econ <- fread("county_econ.csv")   # income, wages, etc.

# Merge
dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by = c("fips","year"), all = TRUE),
             list(ag, demo, econ))

# 2. Variable Construction --------------------------------------
# Dust-Bowl Severity Index (already recorded for 1934–36)
dbi  <- fread("db_severity.csv")   # fips, dbi
dt   <- merge(dt, dbi, by = "fips", all.x = TRUE)

# Treatment indicator
p75  <- quantile(dbi$dbi, .75, na.rm = TRUE)
dt[, treated := as.integer(dbi >= p75)]

# Post indicator
dt[, post := as.integer(year >= 1934)]

# Outcome example: log wheat yield per acre
dt[, l_yield := log(wheat_yield_per_acre)]

# 3. Main DID ----------------------------------------------------
spec_main <- feols(l_yield ~ treated*post + precip + temp |
                     fips + factor(year), data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(spec_main)

# 4. Dynamic Event Study ----------------------------------------
dt[, rel_year := year - 1934]
# omit -1 as baseline
spec_event <- feols(l_yield ~ i(rel_year, treated, ref = -1) + precip + temp |
                       fips + factor(year), data = dt, cluster = ~state)
iplot(spec_event)   # visualization

# 5. Robustness: Border-County Pair DID -------------------------
# identify border pairs
borders <- fread("border_pairs.csv")   # fips, border_pair_id
dtb <- merge(dt, borders, by = "fips")
spec_border <- feols(l_yield ~ treated*post + precip + temp |
                       border_pair_id + factor(year), data = dtb,
                       cluster = ~border_pair_id)
summary(spec_border)
```

==================================================================
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------------
• Short-run (1934-40): 20-30 percent drop in wheat yield per acre; ~10 percent decline in total cropland; 8-15 percent fall in real farm income.  
• Medium term (1940s): partial recovery in yields (still –5 percent) but cropland remains contracted.  
• Long term (1950s–60s): Productivity gap closes; population remains 5-10 percent below counterfactual, indicating persistent out-migration and land-use change.  
Direction: negative contemporaneous effects, with partial but incomplete convergence.

Magnitudes informed by agronomic studies that recorded ≈25 percent topsoil loss translating into ≈0.3 σ yield shocks.



==================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Pre-trend equality visually and statistically verified …………………. 1  
C2: No interference (limited spillovers, addressed by buffers) ………….. 0  
C3: Correct timing/no anticipation …………………………………………. 1  
C4: No simultaneous confounding shocks (controlled with FE & covars) … 0  
C5: Stable unit composition / attrition accounted for …………………… 1  

Total = 3 / 5.  The design is credible but still vulnerable to spillovers and policy confounding, which we attack with robustness and instrumentation.
